chapters.title: The notebooks I never finished.
assets: A page from my notebook, around 2016.
paragraphs: I was a quiet kid at school. If I did not understand something, I usually kept the question to myself. Asking a teacher felt difficult, and homework rarely held my attention long enough for me to finish it.

A class might finish twelve chapters while my notebook stopped at three. That was the kind of gap I remember. My handwriting was untidy, my notebooks were incomplete, and memorising things because I was told to felt tedious. Even so, I usually finished around third in my class, sometimes fourth or fifth.
School saw one version of me. Around people I knew, I had much more to say. There were questions everywhere, and my older brother always seemed willing to explore them with me.

chapters.title: My brother kept my curiosity alive.
assets: Showing my brother what I had made. This photograph comes from the later programming years.
paragraphs: Bhaiya once asked which would hit the ground first: a large brick or a small pebble. I was certain the brick would land first because it was heavier. I expected the little pebble to fall more slowly and arrive later. He held them at the same height and released them together. They landed together. He explained that, when air resistance is negligible, the heavier object does not gain a faster falling acceleration just because it weighs more.

Another time, he asked me to imagine standing at the centre of the roof of the last carriage of a moving train. If I jumped straight up, what would happen? I thought the train would move past me while I was in the air. Because it was the last carriage, I imagined missing the train completely, falling onto the ground and getting badly hurt—or even dying.

He explained that I would already be travelling forward with the train. Jumping would not simply erase that forward motion. A stone tossed from a moving hand helped me picture the idea: it could keep moving forward after leaving the hand. The train question was a thought experiment, not something we did on a train. Everyday objects became ways to understand the world.

Soon I wanted to know about gravity, stars, black holes, time travel and parallel universes. In second grade, I was reading science books meant for much older students. I enjoyed trying to work out their maths problems, too—looking at a triangle and finding a way through it before I knew the formal method.
In a group my brother taught, I learned multiplication tables up to twenty while older students were practising alongside me. I knew everyone there. I felt comfortable enough to try.
That is the part I want to remember most: my brother kept the curiosity of a little kid alive.

chapters.title: I wanted to understand Ben 10.
assets: A frame from one of my English-practice recordings, January 2017.
The Ben 10 watch I made, January 2017.
paragraphs: Before I wrote any code, I was fascinated by phones. My father’s keypad phone could play films. Another phone had Kung Fu Panda. A tiny device could hold these whole worlds—and somehow let us speak to someone far away.

Everything bhaiya downloaded for us came over 2G internet on a Jio keypad phone, including the Doraemon episodes I watched. He would find a particular spot where the phone got reception and wait for a small, low-resolution episode to arrive. Even a tiny file could take hours. I watched the cartoons because he had the patience to get them for me.
During those childhood years, I lost my father.
Later, on an Intex phone, I began watching Ben 10. A friend had told me about the aliens, and I wanted to see everything. But many of the episodes I wanted were only available in English.

At the same time, my brother was learning English through A. J. Hoge’s lessons about listening and imitation. I made the connection: watching Ben 10 could also be my English practice. I listened, repeated the sounds, and recorded myself speaking.
Those recordings still exist. In January 2017, I was practising English on camera and making my own Ben 10 watch. Something I wanted to enjoy had given me a reason to learn.

chapters.title: Three hours. Two numbers.
assets: Our first program: read two numbers, add them, print the sum. July 2017.
The next attempt, which we never got past the errors.
paragraphs: My brother bought a laptop for his studies. His friend Faiz was doing programming, and soon we were trying it too.

Our first program added two numbers. Faiz helped over a voice call while we typed each piece ourselves. A missing semicolon, a bracket in the wrong place, another error. We did not have a fast video connection to make any of it easier.
It took about three hours. The photograph still shows that little program on a blue editor screen.
My brother and I started learning C together. After a while he stopped, but I kept going. I wanted to know what else I could make the computer do.

paragraphs: I followed programming tutorials and worked through loops, operators and patterns. Then I discovered that code could draw. I could put lines on a screen, build a shape from them, and make that shape move.

I wanted to make games. My moving car was a long way from the one I had imagined, but it moved. I drew other cars, an aircraft and a character, and tried to turn sound functions into a simple piano. When I made something I was pleased with, I showed my brother and explained how it worked.
There were plenty of frustrating days too. Moving from Turbo C to Code::Blocks felt like an upgrade, until I spent a whole day trying to run a simple program.

Faiz had also suggested Blender. I tried it in September and found it complicated. Toward the end of the year, watching MJO made me want to create animated videos myself, so I returned to 3D. By November I was also writing HTML in Notepad. Several different paths were opening at once.

paragraphs: In January, I joined SoloLearn. Coding on a phone felt surprisingly social: lessons, challenges, levels, people to compete with. I wanted to learn everything.
I practised HTML, CSS and C++, then moved into more languages as I worked through the challenges. One saved screenshot shows my profile at number one in India for that month.

I also remember hearing about someone reaching Platinum in three days. I made a new account called Beginner and tried to beat that time. As I remember it, I reached Platinum in a day and a half—and the account was banned because my progress was suspected of being cheating.
People in that community came to know me as Beginner. I was still the shy child at school, but here I could spend hours learning, competing and talking about what I was making.

chapters.title: A to Z in 1.510 seconds.
assets: My saved A–Z result. The filename dates it to 13 February 2018.
A Ratatype exercise showing 104 WPM and two typos, 26 January 2018.
paragraphs: Alongside coding, I practised typing with all ten fingers. With enough focus, I could get through some exercises at around a hundred words per minute. One January screenshot shows 104.
Then I found a site where the whole challenge was typing the alphabet. I practised A to Z again and again until my best time reached 1.510 seconds.
I remember being second on the world leaderboard that day. The result screenshot survived; I had named it with the date and how that moment felt.
It was a very particular skill, earned through a lot of repetition. At the time, seeing my practice turn into a result I could measure was an incredible feeling.

chapters.title: Games I could actually play.
paragraphs: Wanting to make games eventually brought me to Unity and C#. The programming and 3D work I had already done started to connect.

I made a Flappy Bird game and played it on my own phone. I also built a small first-person game with a boar chasing the player through a forest. You had to keep moving and shoot before it reached you. I was learning controls, collisions, shooting and game physics by putting them together.

Then I tried something much harder: a racing game with cars that would learn to drive and race alongside a human player. I could follow parts of how training worked, but the mathematics was beyond what I knew. I did not finish that game.

I could not recover the Unity projects after checking my account; I had not kept usable backups. I still remember the feeling of playing something I had built, and how much the unfinished racing project taught me.

Later, when I was learning HTML, CSS and JavaScript more seriously, I made Whack-a-Mole in the browser. I found that game again. Its moving target, countdown and score are a small surviving record of that stage of learning.

chapters.title: A bus became my first paid project.
assets: A still from the saved tour of my bus-conversion model.
The living space inside the model.
paragraphs: I had seen people find paid 3D work online. I asked my brother to help me try. He created an Upwork account, and we searched and applied together.
Our first client needed a model for a bus conversion. I remember starting around October 2020 and spending roughly two months on it. The first payment was $100.
The client liked the work and came back for another addition: a cabin on top of the bus. In total, we earned $180 from that client.

Further work proved difficult to find. I had little professional experience, and my laptop limited the size of projects I could take on. After more applications without another client, I stepped away from 3D freelancing.
The tour of that bus still exists. It records a project I worked through for someone else, delivered, and was paid for.

chapters.title: I chose to focus on the web.
assets: Continuing responsive-design practice with a Frontend Mentor brief, January 2023.
paragraphs: Around this period, Faiz told us about a website commission that had earned him $500. It encouraged me to keep learning. After a pause, I decided to focus on web development properly.

From January 2021 to March 2022, I focused on learning web development seriously. I practised HTML, CSS and JavaScript, then began building with React and working with APIs. Space Tourism, Shopyy, Cryptoverse and an unfinished social media frontend were four projects I spent considerable time on.

These were learning projects, not client products. Space Tourism helped me practise CSS and responsive layouts. Cryptoverse helped me learn API integration. The social media project remained a frontend exercise; I never implemented its backend.

While learning, I reached out to freelancers and found my first frontend freelance work for EazyGrad around January 2022. I built a small set of pages with HTML, CSS and JavaScript micro-interactions. Harigurus followed around February. I kept practising alongside paid work.

chapters.title: When practice became paid work.
paragraphs: Around January 2022, I took on my first frontend freelance work for EazyGrad. The task was a small set of responsive pages using HTML, CSS and JavaScript micro-interactions. I no longer have the exact delivered pages, and the company’s website has since changed.

Harigurus came next, around February 2022. I worked there for about eight months that year, building React booking interfaces, Node.js and Express endpoints, Razorpay payment verification and Twilio SMS confirmations.

Most of my work came through recommendations. People I worked with introduced me to other people. I had less practice applying directly to companies, but I learned what it meant to earn someone’s trust through the work itself.

chapters.title: Making education more affordable.
assets: Helping with a ProCodrr course doubt-solving session, March 2026.
paragraphs: After Harigurus, I moved into social media management and helping develop courses for Anurag Singh’s ProCodrr channel. Making practical education affordable mattered to me.
From 2023 onward, I helped develop course projects, worked through technical ideas and supported learners with their questions. Building the projects and explaining them sharpened my own skills too.
I think about the child who could not ask a teacher when something was unclear. Helping someone else work through a doubt feels especially meaningful from here.

chapters.title: The work you can explore today.
paragraphs: The early experiments grew into projects with interfaces, services and delivery systems I could connect together. Vault Storage is the clearest place to explore that work today.

Vault began with the ProCodrr Node.js storage course. I built out the deployed product and independently developed connected GitHub and Google Drive workspaces, transfers, owner controls, plan rules and billing.
The live site and public repository sit alongside the CI/CD Pipeline Engine and the seven-lab Security Lab. The links let you inspect the work directly.

chapters.title: The next universe: Octoworlds.
paragraphs: As I update this story in November 2026, I am building Octoworlds in Blender: my next universe, and another place for the curiosity that started on our rooftop.
I am also preparing for my next job. ProCodrr gave me meaningful work in affordable education, and my skills and responsibilities grew considerably. My compensation did not grow at the same pace.

I want my next role to match the skills I have developed and the responsibility I can take on, with room to grow in a team whose opportunities reach beyond a local region. This is a next step in the same career.
Different tools. A larger world to build. The same curiosity.
